walkthroughs.body_html:
Physical Geography: Atmosphere — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Physical Geography: Atmosphere brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Physical Geography: Atmosphere.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Tees-Exe Line
Hadrian's Wall

options: Scottish Highlands
Southeast England
Snowdonia
Lake District

mcqs.q: What is the difference between physical and economic water scarcity?
options: Deforestation has no effect on rivers — only rainfall matters.

Physical scarcity is insufficient water supply for demand (e.g. arid regions); economic scarcity is inability to access available water due to lack of infrastructure or investment, despite water being present.
Water scarcity only happens in dry countries.
Economic scarcity means water is too expensive for governments to buy.

mcqs.q: Why does deforestation increase flood risk?
options: Deforestation has no effect on rivers — only rainfall matters.
Deforestation causes floods because trees normally hold water in their branches forever.
Trees intercept rainfall, their roots increase infiltration and transpiration removes water — removing them increases surface runoff and reduces lag time, peaking river levels faster.
Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.

mcqs.q: How do humans affect the carbon cycle?
options: Humans affect the carbon cycle by eating plants.
Humans only affect the carbon cycle by breathing out CO2.
By burning fossil fuels (releasing stored geological carbon to the atmosphere) and deforestation (reducing the biosphere store and releasing carbon).
Economic scarcity means water is too expensive for governments to buy.
